lead.headline: Atoms Cooled to Record Low Temperature Aboard China's Space Station
lead.deck: Scientists on the Tiangong space station chilled about 20,000 rubidium atoms to roughly 10 picokelvins, just above absolute zero.
body: Temperature is really a measure of motion: the slower atoms move, the colder they are. On China's Tiangong space station, scientists have slowed atoms almost to a standstill, reaching about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. Absolute zero is -273.15°C, and this result sits just above it.

The experiment used about 20,000 rubidium atoms and was reported in the journal Science on 5 November. The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter. Laser-based traps held the atoms and reduced their motion, which cooled them.
Why do it in orbit? On Earth, gravity makes a cloud of atoms sag, which weakens the cooling. Microgravity avoids that sag, so the atoms can be cooled further than at home.

Earlier records show the leap: about 52 picokelvins on the International Space Station, and about 38 picokelvins in an Earth drop-tower experiment, where the fall lasts only briefly. Orbit has no such time limit.
One caveat matters: 10 picokelvins is an effective temperature, worked out from how slowly the atoms spread out when allowed to expand, not read from a thermometer.
Ultracold atoms help researchers study exotic states of matter and test basic ideas such as the equivalence principle, which says objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

world.headline: Kyiv Under Fire: Why Power Lines and Bridges Are Targets
world.deck: A night of missiles and drones left Kyiv's residents cold and short of electricity, with talks in Abu Dhabi due within days.
body: Overnight on 6-7 November, missiles and drones came down on Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, and the countryside around it. The targets that suffered most were the things a city needs to function in winter: power stations and a bridge across the Dnipro River.

Kyiv's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reported several waves of ballistic missiles, with several landing on the Northern Bridge. Regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said energy sites were hit in at least three districts. One person died and eight were wounded, one of them a child.

Moscow tells it differently. Russia's defence ministry says its targets were military-industrial sites and energy and transport infrastructure. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, counted 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in the attack.

Cold weather raises the cost. With temperatures near freezing, a France 24 correspondent described Kyiv households living on two to three hours of electricity a day, with no heating and daily water outages. Ukraine's energy ministry said five regions lost power.

Zelensky argues the attack was meant to add pressure before diplomats meet. A three-way meeting in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, is scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday as part of a US-backed peace effort that has produced few results.
Reports add some context: Russia has stepped up air attacks as its ground offensive has largely stalled, and recent weeks have seen attacks on Kyiv's bridges.

world.connect: Geography and economics: a city built on a river depends on bridges, power and water networks, so hitting a few key sites can disrupt millions of lives in winter.

india.headline: Two Cyclones, One Big Bill: Odisha Counts the Cost of Arnab
india.deck: Odisha wants Rs 2,526 crore from the centre to repair storm and flood damage in three districts.
body: The Bay of Bengal sits along India's east coast, and in one week it sent two cyclones ashore. Cyclone Arnab came first, followed by floods in Odisha, and then Cyclone Murasu struck Andhra Pradesh.

Now comes the bill. The Odisha government has sent a memorandum, a formal written request, to the central government. It asks for Rs 2,526 crore for relief and rebuilding in three districts: Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal.

Ganjam shows the scale. All of its blocks were affected, according to a Press Trust of India report. Roads were cut off, houses were damaged and people's livelihoods were hit. The report gives no counts of homes or people, and it reports no deaths.

A word on the money. A crore is ten million, so Rs 2,526 crore is a very large sum, and it is a request, not a payment: the central government still has to decide how much to give. The state's own request and the Congress demand are two different numbers, which shows that how much help is enough is itself a political question.

Notice how the system works. A state asks, and an eight-member central team has already visited the affected areas. Odisha and Andhra Pradesh both lie on India's east coast, so the same Bay of Bengal weather that threatens one can threaten the other within days.

Politicians are already debating how much is needed. Odisha Congress chief Bhakta Charan Das demanded Rs 5,000 crore in central assistance and a national calamity declaration for the floods. BJD chief Naveen Patnaik planned to visit Ganjam on Saturday, 7 November.
Compare the two storms. Arnab and Murasu both came within days of each other, and reporters called Murasu the second cyclone to strike the region in a week.

The second storm landed further south. Cyclone Murasu crossed the coast near Ongole in Prakasam district at about 1 am on Tuesday, 3 November. Authorities planned to move about 30,000 people to safety, and none had been reported hurt at the time.
Trees and electricity poles were uprooted, fishing boats were wrecked and standing crops were hit in Prakasam and Bapatla districts.

us.headline: Trump Names Stephen Miller Chief of Staff as Democrats Prepare to Take Congress
us.deck: The new chief of staff starts on Monday, 9 November, days after Republicans lost the House and the Senate.
body: The White House chief of staff is the president's top aide, who in general manages the schedule and coordinates senior staff. On Friday, 6 November, President Trump named Stephen Miller to the job on Truth Social, saying he would take over starting Monday, 9 November.

Miller is 41. He is currently deputy chief of staff for policy and also homeland security advisor, and he has been one of Trump's closest aides for more than a decade. He replaces Susie Wiles, 69, the first woman to hold the job. Friday was her last day, and she is moving to the Trump Political Operation.

Miller's record is the reason for the debate. He drove the mass deportation programme, which often involved raids by masked agents. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer vowed to oppose his appointment.

The timing follows a political shift. Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate to Democrats in the 4 November midterms, so Trump now faces a divided government for his last two years.
Why they lost is itself disputed. Vice President Vance said the Iran war was the reason, and Trump said what Vance had said was largely true.
Democrats take control of Congress in early January. With the majority comes subpoena power, the legal power to demand documents and testimony, and Democrats plan a long list of investigations.
The Constitution still limits both sides. Most legislation needs 60 votes in the Senate to get past a filibuster, and a presidential veto can only be overridden with two-thirds of both chambers.

Democrats' early priorities include restoring enhanced health subsidies under the Affordable Care Act, reversing Medicaid cuts, reasserting Congress's authority over tariffs and forcing votes to end the Iran war.

science_and_technology.headline: How Octopuses Squeeze Through Holes Smaller Than Their Heads
science_and_technology.deck: Filmed experiments show octopuses fitting through tight holes in careful steps, which could help design soft robots.
body: An octopus has no bones, yet it can slip through a gap that looks far too small. A study in the Journal of Experimental Biology filmed three common octopuses and four Mayan octopuses to see exactly how they do it.

The researchers needed a measuring stick. They used the distance between each octopus's eyes as a stand-in for the size of its most rigid cartilage, which surrounds the brain. Then they offered acrylic boxes with holes slightly smaller or slightly larger than that distance.

When the hole was wider, the octopuses took three steps over a few seconds. First one or two arms went through. Then a couple more were threaded in. Finally the arms already through pulled the head and remaining arms after them.

Notice what the two routes have in common. In both, the soft arms go first and the stiffest part of the body, the head around the brain, comes last. That is why the eye-to-eye distance was a useful measuring stick: the rigid cartilage is the part that has to fit.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses used four steps. They pushed all their arms through first, and only then squeezed the head and the bulbous mantle, the body part behind the head, through the gap.
The two species behaved differently. Mayan octopuses were more cautious, and faced with the narrower hole they usually ignored it instead of trying to fit through.
A possible explanation comes from habitat. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas and rarely need to squeeze through holes, which may explain their reluctance.

A good scientist also asks how far a result can be trusted. This test used only three common octopuses and four Mayan octopuses, so it shows how these animals behaved in these boxes. It does not prove that every octopus, or every kind of opening, works the same way.
The work could help engineers. The team hopes the findings will inspire soft robots that change shape to reach tight spaces, since current hole-fitting robots tend to be snake-shaped.
There is more to learn. Robyn Crook of San Francisco State University, who was not involved, suggests that slits or tubes may call for different strategies than round holes.

economics.headline: A Narrow Sea, a Few Exceptions: Oil Flows at the Strait of Hormuz
economics.deck: Iran says some countries' ships may cross, yet traffic in the waterway remains far below its pre-war level.
body: Economists call a place that everything must pass through a bottleneck, and the Strait of Hormuz is one. In October, 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude oil passed through it, according to the analysis firm Kpler. India took 13 percent of that oil and China about 42 percent.

Then came a statement from Tehran. Amir Hayat Moqaddam, who is deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the ISNA news agency on Tuesday that vessels from India, China, Iraq and Qatar are free to cross. In return, he said, Iran will charge fees to Indian and Chinese ships; Qatari ships go through free.

To understand why this matters, go back to the war. It began on 28 February as a US-Israel war on Iran. Iran effectively closed the strait early on, and in July the US reimposed a naval blockade on Iran's southern ports.

US Central Command says that blockade covers every vessel going in or out of Iranian ports, and it is unclear whether Washington accepts the new exemptions. The IG Group analyst quoted by Al Jazeera said they make only a limited difference to oil markets for now.

The numbers show how far traffic has fallen. In its weekly report, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre counted 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits, about 65 percent below levels before the conflict. At least 11 ships were attacked near the strait during the week to 6 November, and three of them sank.

A permit does not equal safety. A Qatari LNG carrier, the Al Mayeda, was struck by unidentified objects on 30 October, and more than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October the worst month.

Talks continue in the background. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says he spoke with 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours, including those of Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and he restated Iran's seven demands to reopen the strait.
Fires and mines are still part of the picture. Iran's navy said a tanker with its transponder off caught fire in the eastern strait after hitting a mine; Washington says the mines have been cleared.

explainer.title: Why does gravity matter to cold atoms?
body: To cool atoms, scientists use lasers to hold them in a trap and reduce their motion. Slower atoms are colder. On Earth, however, gravity makes a cloud of atoms sag, which weakens the cooling.

In orbit, atoms experience microgravity, so the sag is avoided. Drop towers do the same trick for a few moments while an experiment falls, but they are limited by how long the fall lasts. A space station has no such time limit. That is why researchers can reach about 10 picokelvins there, compared with about 38 picokelvins in a drop tower.

lead.headline: Atoms Get Super Cold in Space
body: Scientists on China's Tiangong space station made atoms very, very cold. They reached about 10 picokelvins. That is 10 trillionths of a kelvin, just above absolute zero.
They used about 20,000 rubidium atoms. Lasers held the atoms and slowed them down. Slower atoms are colder.
In space, gravity does not make the atom cloud sag. So the atoms can get colder than on Earth. The result was reported on 5 November.

world.headline: Strikes Hit Kyiv Before Peace Talks
body: Russia sent missiles and drones at Kyiv overnight. They damaged energy sites and a big bridge over the Dnipro River. One person was killed and eight were hurt.
It was near freezing in Kyiv. People there had only two to three hours of electricity a day. Zelensky said Russia launched 172 drones and 36 missiles.
New talks between the sides are planned in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

india.headline: Odisha Asks for Help After Storms
body: Two cyclones hit India's east coast in a week. Cyclone Arnab came first. Then Cyclone Murasu came ashore in Andhra Pradesh.
Odisha has asked the central government for Rs 2,526 crore to fix damage from the storm and floods. The money is for three districts: Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal.
An eight-member central team has visited the area. In Ganjam, roads were cut off and houses were damaged.

us.headline: A New Chief of Staff for the White House
body: President Trump named Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. Miller is 41. He starts on Monday, 9 November. He replaces Susie Wiles, who is 69.
The chief of staff is the president's top aide. The choice comes after Republicans lost both the House and the Senate in the midterms. Democrats take control of Congress in early January.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said he will oppose Miller's appointment.

science_and_technology.headline: How Octopuses Fit Through Tiny Holes
body: Octopuses can squeeze through very small gaps. Scientists filmed them going through holes in boxes.
For a wide hole, they pushed one or two arms through first. Then more arms went in. Last, the arms pulled the head and the rest of the body through.
For a narrower hole, common octopuses pushed all their arms through first. The study could help engineers design soft robots.

economics.headline: Which Ships Can Cross Hormuz?
body: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea route for oil. An Iranian lawmaker said ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar can pass.
But the sea is still dangerous. At least 11 ships were attacked in one week, and three sank. Traffic is about 65 percent below normal.
Some countries are trying to help. Iran's foreign minister said he spoke with 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours.
